items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Podcast conversation with Kyla Scanlon and Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin (transcript on Kyla's Newsletter)
items.quote: We’re not in a place where we’re making large policy moves.
items.summary: Daly said the Fed cut to offset a softer labor market while inflation still prints above target, and that policy is now in a fine-tuning phase: a stone's throw from neutral for some forecasters, with a little more room for others. She stressed nimbleness and looking past single data points.
items.score_note: Fine-tuning near neutral, no lean on the next move. The Substack page is dated Jan 9, 2026; the SF Fed coverage post linking to it is stamped Jan 6, so the recording is from the first days of January.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: MNI webcast, Q&A moderated by Pedro da Costa (video only on stlouisfed.org; quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: I see little reason for near-term further easing of policy.
items.summary: Musalem said the 3.50%-3.75% policy rate is roughly neutral and need not fall unless the resilient labor market starts to fail or inflation falls faster than expected. He said it is too early to call a higher-productivity regime and too early to "outsource" the job of returning inflation to 2%. In the same webcast he said he expects the next Fed chair to stay committed to the dual mandate.
items.score_note: Explicit pushback on near-term cuts while markets priced further easing; no hint of hikes.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy", Economic Club of Kansas City
items.quote: With inflation pressures still evident, my preference would be to keep monetary policy modestly restrictive.
items.summary: Schmid explained his dissents against the October and December 2025 cuts: inflation near 3% is too high, cuts would do little for a labor market cooled by structural forces, and policy is no longer very restrictive because the neutral rate has risen. He said he sees little reason to lower the policy rate further. Headline-level wire reports of the Q&A add that he sees little reason to cut and puts full employment at roughly 3.5%-4.5% unemployment.
items.score_note: Pushes back on further cuts and says policy is not very restrictive; does not call for a hike.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: LinkedIn post (Reuters reprint on a radio-station syndication page; the LinkedIn original was not opened)
items.quote: We will need to be deliberate as we calibrate policy to achieve both price stability and full employment
items.summary: Daly wrote that incoming data look promising: growth projections are solid, the labor market is stabilizing and inflation is expected to improve over the year. She said policy is in a good place to respond to however the economy evolves and that calibration should be deliberate.
items.score_note: "Good place" and deliberate calibration ahead of the January hold; no lean.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "U.S. Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy" and moderated Q&A, Arkansas Business Forecast Luncheon, Rogers, Ark. (University of Arkansas CBER)
items.quote: With inflation above target and the risks to the outlook evenly balanced, I believe it would be unadvisable to lower the rate into accommodative territory at this time.
items.summary: Two days after the January hold, Musalem said he supported keeping the funds rate at 3.5%-3.75%, called that setting neutral, and said risks to the outlook are evenly balanced. He expects growth at or above trend and inflation to resume falling toward 2% as tariff effects fade, but said cutting into accommodative territory would be unadvisable.
items.score_note: Hold with balanced risks would be 0, but he explicitly pushes back on further cuts (unadvisable to lower the rate into accommodative territory) at a time markets priced cuts; scored +1 on the rubric line "pushes back on cut talk". Borderline with 0.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview with Ann Saphir (Reuters exclusive, Yahoo Finance copy)
items.quote: I was supportive of that decision, but frankly, I thought you could make a case for going ahead and taking a little more off
items.summary: Daly said she supported the January hold but that a case could be made for another cut, and that she leans toward additional cuts in 2026, whether one or two being hard to say. She is a little more worried about the labor market than about inflation and called the job market precarious; cutting requires real confidence that tariff effects roll off and inflation is falling, or more worry about jobs than the data now show.
items.score_note: Leans toward one or two more cuts and puts labor-market risk first, but supported the hold and sets conditions; -1 rather than -2.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "Monetary Policy and the Economic Outlook", Economic Forum of Albuquerque, N.M.
items.quote: In my view, further rate cuts risk allowing high inflation to persist even longer.
items.summary: Schmid said demand is outpacing supply with inflation closer to 3% than 2%, so a somewhat restrictive stance is appropriate, and the funds rate is arguably no longer restraining activity much, if at all. He supported the January hold. On the balance sheet, he said the reserve-management bill purchases begun in December are not easing and that the Fed should keep shrinking its MBS holdings and shorten its Treasury duration.
items.score_note: Opposes further cuts on inflation grounds and doubts policy is restrictive; no call for a hike.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Keynote "The AI Moment? Possibilities, Productivity, and Policy" and conversation with Ed Ludlow, Silicon Valley Leadership Group / San Jose State University (official Q&A transcript)
items.quote: So right now we’re modestly restrictive, slightly restrictive, depending on who you talk to.
items.summary: In the prepared speech Daly drew on the 1990s, when the Greenspan FOMC stayed patient as productivity rose, and said policy must be forward-looking but evidence-based on AI. In the Q&A she said policy is modestly or slightly restrictive, with roughly 75 basis points to go to a neutral rate near 3%, but that inflation needs to come down first.
items.score_note: Describes policy as slightly restrictive with room to go to neutral (a mild easing bias) but conditions it on inflation falling; no call for a near-term move, so 0 rather than -1.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: In Conversation: Mary C. Daly with Rob Kaplan (Harvard Business School audience, SF Fed; official transcript)
items.quote: But our dual mandate goals that are price stability and full employment, both seem to be in a good place.
items.summary: Daly said the 75 basis points of cuts in late 2025 put the labor market in a better place, inflation keeps coming down outside tariff-affected goods, and policy is in a good place. She said the Fed should neither constrain an economy that may get a productivity lift from AI nor forget inflation is above target.
items.score_note: Policy "in a good place", both mandates in a good place, no lean on the next move.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Fox Business interview with Edward Lawrence, 'The Claman Countdown', live from the St. Louis Fed Economy Museum (video page)
items.quote: well positioned
items.summary: Video-only interview. Fox Business's page title quotes Musalem as saying policy is 'well positioned' amid rate-cut speculation; the page says he discussed the Supreme Court tariff ruling, Warsh's nomination, monetary policy and data. A Reuters reprint of the same interview (https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-02-20/feds-musalem-tariff-ruling-could-mean-uncertainty) quotes him only on tariffs: one-for-one replacement tariffs would leave his forecast unchanged but the transition could bring a period of uncertainty for companies.
items.score_note: Only a two-word quotation in the outlet headline is available as text; "well positioned" signals comfort with holding. Thin evidence, scored 0 rather than inferring a lean from the video.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Moderated Q&A "Role of the Federal Reserve in the St. Louis Region", Missouri Athletic Club Speaker Series, St. Louis (video only on stlouisfed.org; quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: these two risks in my assessment are roughly balanced right now
items.summary: Musalem said the current policy rate appropriately balances risks. His baseline has inflation heading back toward 2% later in the year and the labor market stabilizing; more layoffs with low job creation could worsen the labor market (not his base case), and inflation could stay higher for longer.
items.score_note: Hold with explicitly balanced two-sided risks.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Appearance before the Economic Club of Colorado (Reuters reprint)
items.quote: I think we have work to do on the inflation side of things
items.summary: Schmid said the Fed has work to do on inflation while employment is in a pretty good place; Reuters noted he did not say how policy should respond. On the balance sheet he said the debate is about the right level of reserves, that the Fed's MBS holdings keep mortgage rates probably 75 to 100 basis points lower than otherwise, and (per a later Reuters story) that the long duration of the portfolio creates a distortion.
items.score_note: Inflation named as the unfinished side of the mandate with employment fine; no explicit rate call, so a mild +1.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy", Metro Denver Executive Club, Denver, Colo.
items.quote: Overall, with inflation still running hot, it appears that demand is outpacing supply across much of the economy.
items.summary: Schmid said the labor market looks in balance while inflation remains closer to 3% than 2% and the Fed cannot be complacent after nearly five years above target. He argued that demand-led growth, including aging-related health care spending, is not disinflationary and that AI-led supply gains are not here yet.
items.score_note: Inflation is the dominant concern and the framing argues against easing, but the text gives no explicit rate-path statement; +1 is the mild hawkish lean.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Panel discussion presentation on the value of private-sector data (official transcript)
items.quote: And this just reminds us that monetary policy is a contextual decision that takes a lot of evidence, a lot of science, a lot of practice, but also some judgment
items.summary: Daly discussed how the FOMC has used private-sector data (ADP, Zillow rents, PriceStats) alongside official statistics, with examples from the 1990s, 2020 and 2025. No statement on the current rate path.
items.score_note: Official panel remarks about data sources; no usable stance on the rate path.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' interview with Steve Liesman after the February jobs report (quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: But we also have inflation printing above target and oil prices rising.
items.summary: After a weak February jobs report, Daly said hopes that the labor market was steadying may have been too much, but inflation is above target and oil prices are rising, so both goals are at risk and the Fed must keep its eye on both.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided: labor weaker, inflation and oil higher; no stated lean on rates.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: LinkedIn post (Reuters reprint; the LinkedIn original was not opened)
items.quote: in a good place, we need to remain flexible
items.summary: Daly wrote that unless the Iran conflict resolves quickly and the Fed can look through a temporary oil price rise, there is "no single most-likely path" for rates: a protracted conflict raises the risk of both higher inflation and a weaker labor market. Full sentence in the reprint: "With policy in a good place, we need to remain flexible, able to respond to rapidly evolving risks."
items.score_note: No directional lean; two-sided risks and flexibility. The quote is a fragment because the reprint embeds invisible characters elsewhere in the sentence.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy", Rotary Club of Oklahoma City, Okla.
items.quote: With inflation already running hot, now is not the time to assume that the inflation from higher oil prices will be transitory.
items.summary: After the Iran-related oil price jump, Schmid said he is more focused on inflation risks than on growth: inflation was near 3% before the shock, progress has stalled, and higher energy prices will raise core as well as headline inflation. He said the Fed must follow through with policy actions that validate stable inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Inflation risk explicitly dominates and he rejects looking through the oil shock; stops short of calling for a hike.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy" and moderated Q&A, American Enterprise Institute, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: Policy is well positioned to address risks to both dual mandate objectives, and I expect the current setting of the policy rate will remain appropriate for some time.
items.summary: Musalem said he supported the January and March holds; the real policy rate is in the lower part of the neutral range and the current rate will likely stay appropriate for some time. Risks tilt both to a weaker labor market and to more persistent above-target inflation after the Middle East energy shock. He laid out both directions: he could support easing if labor weakens with inflation expectations contained, and could support raising the rate if core inflation or longer-term expectations move persistently higher; easing on the mere prospect of AI productivity would be risky.
items.score_note: Explicit extended hold with two-sided risks and symmetric conditions for a cut or a hike. Warnings about looking through supply shocks lean slightly hawkish, but the stated stance is balanced.
items.ai_quote: For now, recent stress in private credit markets appears mostly due to liquidity issues and some marking down of net asset values, rather than widespread credit quality problems.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: SF Fed Blog essay "Monetary Policy in a Slow (to No) Growth Labor Market"
items.quote: And with inflation already printing above target, policymakers will have to be very clear about how movement towards our mandated goals will be achieved.
items.summary: Daly wrote that with labor force growth near zero, zero or negative monthly job growth can be consistent with full employment, so ratios such as the unemployment rate are better gauges than payroll counts. Uncertainty about potential growth raises the risk of holding policy too loose or too tight, and communication gets harder with inflation above target.
items.score_note: Structural essay with no stated lean on the rate path; the point that weak payrolls need not signal slack mildly argues against reacting with cuts, but risks are framed as two-sided.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Keynote "Regionalism at the Federal Reserve: Many Voices, One Purpose" and conversation with Chip Childs, St. George Area Chamber of Commerce, Utah (official transcript of the conversation)
items.quote: So from my vantage point today, I see the underlying fundamentals of the economy as really in a good place.
items.summary: The prepared speech (https://www.frbsf.org/news-and-media/speeches/mary-c-daly/2026/04/many-voices-one-purpose/) is about the Fed's regional structure and independence. In the conversation Daly said the economy's fundamentals are solid, it is too early to judge the effect of the war and oil prices on inflation, and longer-run inflation expectations are well behaved. No statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: Official speech on Fed structure; outlook comments only, nothing usable on the policy rate path.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview given the day before the March CPI release (Reuters exclusive published April 10; quotes read in a same-day Reuters story)
items.quote: We had work to do before we had the oil price shock; with the oil price shock, the work just takes longer
items.summary: Daly said a higher CPI number would surprise no one and need not change the plan to hold or perhaps cut: if the ceasefire holds and oil falls, the Fed could eventually lower rates; if oil and inflation are sticky it can hold and wait. She thought a surge that forces the Fed to chase inflation with hikes is less likely, and said the Fed could just be holding steady until it knows the job is getting done. The SF Fed summary of the interview says she called policy in a "good place".
items.score_note: Holding pattern; she ranks a cut above a hike among the alternatives, a mild dovish tilt, but the stated stance is wait.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview (listed by the St. Louis Fed as April 15, 2026; quotes read in a later Reuters story that cites the interview)
items.quote: is in a good place, and I think it's probably going to be appropriate to maintain policy at this level for some time
items.summary: Musalem said policy is in a good place and should probably stay at this level for some time. He said a long period of high oil prices could lift core inflation, at which point the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations would become relevant and "it might be appropriate to raise rates"; for now medium- to long-term expectations are well anchored. The original Reuters headline (reuters.com, not readable here) says the oil shock is likely to keep core inflation near 3%.
items.score_note: Extended hold is the stated stance; the hike is conditional on de-anchoring that he says has not happened. Leans hawkish but nearer 0. Date is the interview date as listed on stlouisfed.org; the page read is the April 27 Reuters story.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Conversation with Alex Mehran Sr., UC Berkeley Fisher Center for Real Estate & Urban Economics (official transcript)
items.quote: right now, policy’s in a very good place, slightly restrictive, not constraining the economy so much that the labor market’s faltering
items.summary: Daly said that before the oil shock she expected one or two more cuts toward a neutral rate around 3%; now, with oil lifting inflation, policy is slightly restrictive and in a very good place for wait-and-see. Scenarios: hold all year; raise if inflation really took off (not her modal outlook); or cut as in the March SEP (one cut) if the labor market falters or the conflict ends quickly. She would not be surprised by market pricing of zero cuts this year.
items.score_note: Explicit wait-and-see hold with a hike and a cut scenario both described; her earlier easing bias is suspended, not reversed.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Q&A with Gordon Fellows, Mississippi Bankers Association annual convention, Point Clear, Ala. (official transcript)
items.quote: In my understanding, that risk has been shifting toward more risk on the inflation side than the employment side.
items.summary: Musalem said the labor market has stabilized while inflation runs meaningfully above target (March core PCE 3.2%, headline 3.5%) and longer-term expectations are drifting up. He put the real funds rate at about 0.5% or lower, below the 1% long-run neutral, so policy is neutral or slightly accommodative. He sees plausible scenarios for holding for some time, for cutting, and for higher rates.
items.score_note: Says the balance of risks has shifted toward inflation and that policy is neutral to slightly accommodative in real terms; still lists hold, cut and hike scenarios, so +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview with Michael McKee (auto-generated transcript published with the Bloomberg Talks podcast clip, https://omny.fm/shows/bloomberg-talks/san-francisco-fed-president-mary-daly-talks-fed)
items.quote: the inflation expectations being well anchored is an important component of our ability to be patient
items.summary: Daly said the real signal from the April meeting is that everyone agreed to hold, and that the statement wording matters less than the FOMC's actions. It is too early to say the cutting cycle is over: if the conflict ends and oil falls, slightly restrictive policy keeps pushing inflation down. She does not see medium- or long-run inflation expectations drifting, sees little pass-through beyond energy surcharges, and said overreacting can damage the economy as much as underreacting.
items.score_note: Patient hold; plays down the easing-bias dissents and still leaves cuts possible, but gives no lean for the next move. Transcript is machine-generated; the Bloomberg text story (https://news.bgov.com/banking-law/feds-daly-says-statement-language-is-less-important-than-action) confirms the date and the statement-language quote.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Policy panel presentation on shocks and monetary policy, Hoover Institution Monetary Policy Conference 2026 (with Bowman, Waller, Goolsbee; official transcript)
items.quote: It says you’re going to have more persistent inflation pressure.
items.summary: Daly questioned the conventional wisdom of looking through supply shocks. Her inflation dashboard supported looking through the tariff shock, but with the oil shock on top, data through April are starting to show red where expected, and clogged supply chains could make inflation pressure more persistent. She gave no rate prescription.
items.score_note: Flags rising risk of persistent inflation pressure from the oil shock (hawkish tilt) but stops at "more data to watch" with no policy conclusion; nearer 0 than +1.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "Leveraging Modern Payments Infrastructure in Community Banking", Future of Banking Conference, Kansas City, Mo.
items.quote: However, I see continued inflation as the most pressing risk to the economy.
items.summary: Mostly a payments and FedNow speech. In a short outlook passage Schmid said the economy is resilient and the labor market is functioning, but inflation is still too high and is the most pressing risk.
items.score_note: Only a brief outlook passage; inflation named as the dominant risk, no rate-path statement.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Keynote "How Should the Promise of Higher Productivity Growth Change the Reality of Monetary Policy Today?" and Q&A (moderator Claire Jones, FT), Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland
items.quote: A better policy would be to lean against demand and inflation pressures today.
items.summary: Musalem argued it would be risky to rely on future AI-driven productivity gains to solve today's inflation problem. He noted the real policy rate is below the FOMC's long-run neutral, inflation is meaningfully above target and longer-term inflation expectations are creeping higher, and said holding policy rates too low could push long-term rates up. He called for a vigilant policy focused on restoring price stability and said he would adjust only if evidence shows productivity is pulling inflation to target. In the Q&A (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-28/fed-policymakers-eye-rate-hike-scenarios-ai-debate-deepens) he said "If we don't see disinflation in the next one to two quarters, that would concern me" and that risks have tilted more toward inflation than the labor market.
items.score_note: Inflation risk dominates and he says policy should lean against demand; says the real rate is below neutral. No explicit call for a hike in the prepared text, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg TV interview with Stephanie Flanders at the Reykjavik Economic Conference (auto-generated transcript published with the Bloomberg Talks podcast clip, https://omny.fm/shows/bloomberg-talks/feds-alberto-musalem-talks-fed-policy)
items.quote: There is a scenario where inflation remains high, there's no disinflation in the next quarter or two, and in that scenario, the economy will probably require a hike.
items.summary: Musalem said the real policy rate is around 0.5%, below the 1% the Committee sees as neutral, so policy is at or slightly below long-run neutral. He supported the April hold but thought the statement's easing bias was no longer consistent with the outlook and a balance of risks that has shifted toward inflation. Hike, cut or hold depends on the scenario: no disinflation in a quarter or two would probably require a hike; a material weakening in the second half would mean no hikes, maybe a cut. He said the probability of considering a rate increase "has to be greater than zero", and that shrinking the balance sheet is better done by reducing reserve demand than by cutting supply.
items.score_note: Open to hiking and wanted the easing bias removed, but frames a hike as scenario-dependent rather than needed now; +1 not +2. Transcript is machine-generated (names are garbled in places); the quoted sentence matches the Reuters account of the interview.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Local and the Global in Monetary Policy", Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland (discussion moderated by Stephanie Flanders)
items.quote: We must continue to signal our commitment to price stability and our willingness to take the actions necessary to achieve our mandate.
items.summary: Schmid said the oil disruption is adding to inflation (CPI 3.8% in the 12 months to April, 2.8% excluding energy), that with inflation above 2% for over five years it is not the time to let down the guard, and that he places little stock in the latest run-up being transitory. He sees the labor market in balance; inflation is his primary concern in setting policy. In comments after the speech (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-29/feds-schmid-warns-against-viewing-oil-shock-transitory) he said "We're not very restrictive at this stage" and that officials need to start considering what tools they have to make policy a little more restrictive, including looking at the balance sheet again.
items.score_note: Inflation dominates; in Q&A he said policy is not very restrictive and tools to add restriction should be considered, depending on the oil shock. Open to tightening but no call for an immediate hike; +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria' interview with Maria Bartiromo (quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: there's no urgency to make an adjustment
items.summary: Daly said policy is in a good place and there is no urgency to adjust rates; any future move may hinge on when the Iran war ends. If oil futures drift up because the conflict persists, that would change her inflation outlook. She is watching whether services firms start raising prices and so far sees little of that outside fuel-intensive industries.
items.score_note: Comfortable holding while several colleagues that week talked about hikes; conditional concern on oil only.

coverage_notes: Presidents and occasions were taken from each bank's own lists, then cross-checked against wire coverage. Musalem: every entry on the St. Louis Fed 'Remarks and Speeches' list dated Jan 1 to May 31, 2026 was opened (9 policy occasions: Jan 13 MNI, Jan 30 Arkansas, Feb 20 Fox Business, Feb 25 Missouri Athletic Club, Apr 1 AEI, Apr 15 Reuters, May 6 Mississippi Bankers, May 28 Reykjavik speech, May 28 Bloomberg TV); the list shows no remarks in March (only a March 2 agriculture roundtable and an April 8-9 Memphis visit, no texts). Schmid: the kansascityfed.org sitemap was filtered for /speeches/ pages by Jeff Schmid (Jan 15, Feb 11, Mar 3, Mar 31, May 14, May 29); the other /speeches/ entries in the window are staff presentations. Wire coverage added Feb 25 (Economic Club of Colorado). Nothing was found for Schmid in April. Daly: SF Fed speeches, events and news-coverage posts for the window were pulled through the site's WordPress API and every Daly entry was opened; event dates and times come from the event pages (Pacific time converted to ET). Transcripts are posted for Feb 17, Feb 19, Mar 6, Apr 8, Apr 17 and May 8. Wire layer: Kitco's off-the-wire sitemap lists every Reuters reprint by date; all 864 Fed- and market-related reprints dated Jan 1 to Jun 2, 2026 were downloaded and searched for the three names, and a headline feed (Newsquawk via StockNow) was used to confirm that no occasion was missed.
